query: Reported superconducting high-entropy alloys are dominated by Nb-Ta matrices, while other studies concern titanium-rich systems based on heavy transition metals and partly ordered systems. Consequently, these precedents do not establish what controls superconductivity in high-entropy alloys outside the best-studied material classes. Within the defining constraint of a solid solution containing at least five elements at no less than 5 atomic percent each, what governs superconducting behavior in such an uncharacterized high-entropy alloy, and why? State one testable mechanistic hypothesis, a controlled comparison against the starting material, predicted observations relative to the baseline, applicable boundary conditions, the earlier evidence supporting the hypothesis, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In disordered, single‐phase high‐entropy alloy superconductors, the superconducting critical parameters (Tc and Hc2) are primarily governed by the effective valence electron count, which modulates the electron–phonon coupling strength and density of states at the Fermi level, while the intrinsic chemical disorder provides scattering centers that can enhance or suppress Cooper pairing. Thus, systematically tuning the electron count via compositional adjustments (while retaining the disordered solid‐solution BCC structure) will yield predictable changes in Tc and Hc2.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogeneous, single–phase high–entropy alloy superconducting material (e.g. a BCC lattice containing ≥5 elements at ≥5 at.% each) such as the Nb–Ti–Zr–Ta–Hf family.
generation.intervention: Systematic adjustment of the alloy composition to vary the effective valence electron count (for instance, by slightly altering the ratios of Nb, Ti, Zr, Ta, and Hf) while preserving the high configurational disorder and single-phase BCC structure.
generation.conditions: Measurements performed at ambient pressure and low temperatures (near and below the superconducting transition) in samples processed to ensure chemical homogeneity.
generation.structural_mediator: The disordered BCC lattice, whose local chemical environment (and any incipient short-range order) influences electron scattering and thus mediates the electron–phonon coupling responsible for superconductivity.
generation.mechanism: Variations in the effective valence electron count alter the density of electronic states near the Fermi level and the electron–phonon interaction strength. In turn, this affects the superconducting pairing potential. Meanwhile, the high configurational disorder provides scattering centers that can act as both pair breakers and enhancers of pairing interactions, with an optimum balance yielding maximal Tc and upper critical field.
generation.predicted_outcome: As the effective electron count is tuned, the superconducting transition temperature (Tc) and upper critical field (Hc2) will vary in a systematic manner – increasing up to an optimal electron concentration where pairing is maximized, then possibly decreasing if excessive pair-breaking scattering sets in. The observed trends should correlate with changes in electron–phonon coupling indicators.
generation.baseline: The state of a known HEA superconductor (e.g., Nb0.34Ti0.33Zr0.14Ta0.11Hf0.08) exhibiting a Tc around 7.5 K and a high upper critical field, representing the performance of the baseline disordered BCC alloy.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to be valid only for high–entropy alloys that form homogeneous, single–phase solid solutions (with at least 5 constituents each present at no less than 5 at.%), and it may not apply in multiphase or partially ordered systems where other mechanisms (e.g. magnetic pair breaking or intergranular effects) dominate.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative relationship between effective electron count and superconducting parameters (Tc and Hc2) remains uncertain, along with the balance between beneficial electron–phonon coupling and detrimental pair-breaking scattering from disorder. Further experimental and theoretical studies are needed to pinpoint the optimum electron concentration and to detail the role of chemical inhomogeneities.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a series of high–entropy alloy superconductors based on a BCC solid solution (e.g., modifying the Nb–Ti–Zr–Ta–Hf system) by carefully varying the relative concentrations of the constituent elements to systematically adjust the effective valence electron count. Ensure that each composition remains a homogeneous, single–phase alloy. Measure the superconducting transition temperature (Tc) and upper critical field (Hc2) via magnetization and resistivity experiments across the series.
measurements: Superconducting transition temperature (Tc) via resistivity drop and susceptibility measurements
Upper critical field (Hc2) via magnetic field–dependent resistivity or magnetization
Electronic density of states near the Fermi level (potentially via tunneling spectroscopy)
Assessment of electron–phonon coupling strength (from specific heat or spectroscopic measurements)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If systematic variations in the effective valence electron count do not produce corresponding and predictable trends in Tc and Hc2 – for example, if no optimum correlation is observed or if changes in Tc/Hc2 are within experimental noise and unrelated to composition – then the hypothesis that electron count primarily governs superconductivity in these HEAs would be falsified.

Enhanced Superconducting Critical Parameters in a New High-Entropy Alloy Nb0.34Ti0.33Zr0.14Ta0.11Hf0.08

Abstract: The structural and physical properties of the new titanium- and niobium-rich type-A high-entropy alloy (HEA) superconductor Nb0.34Ti0.33Zr0.14Ta0.11Hf0.08 (in at.%) were studied by X-ray powder diffraction, energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy, magnetization, electrical resistivity, and specific heat measurements. In addition, electronic structure calculations were performed using two complementary methods: the Korringa–Kohn–Rostoker Coherent Potential Approximation (KKR-CPA) and the Projector Augmented Wave (PAW) within Density Functional Theory (DFT). The results obtained indicate that the alloy exhibits type II superconductivity with a critical temperature close to 7.5 K, an intermediate electron–phonon coupling, and an upper critical field of 12.2(1) T. This finding indicates that Nb0.34Ti0.33Zr0.14Ta0.11Hf0.08 has one of the highest upper critical fields among all known HEA superconductors.

Robust zero resistance in a superconducting high-entropy alloy at pressures up to 190 GPa

Abstract: SignificanceHigh-entropy alloys (HEAs) are made from multiple transition-metal elements in equimolar or near-equimolar ratios. The elements in HEAs arrange themselves randomly on the crystallographic positions of a simple lattice. In addition to their excellent mechanical properties, one HEA has been reported to display superconductivity. In this work, we report that the Ta–Nb–Hf–Zr–Ti high-entropy alloy superconductor exhibits extraordinarily robust zero-resistance superconductivity under pressure up to 190.6 GPa.
